The '''2001–2002 Scottish Premier League''' (known as the '''2001–2002 [[Bank of Scotland]] Premier League''' for sponsorship reasons) was the fourth season of the [[Scottish Premier League]], the top level of [[Association football|football]] in Scotland. It began on 28 July 2001 and concluded on 12 May 2002.<ref name="SPFL Archive">{{cite web|url=https://spfl.co.uk/premiership/archive/2001-2002|title=Scottish Premier League Archive 2001/2002|access-date=6 February 2018|publisher=[[Scottish Professional Football League]]|archive-date=7 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207122141/https://spfl.co.uk/premiership/archive/2001-2002|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] were the defending champions, and successfully retained the title with a 5–1 victory over [[Livingston F.C.|Livingston]] on 6 April 2002.<ref name="Celtic win title">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/1912027.stm|title=Five-star Celtic claim title|date=6 April 2002|access-date=6 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref>

==Changes from 2000–01 season==
===Winter break===
This season was the first season since the Scottish Premier League (SPL) began in [[1998–99 Scottish Premier League|1998–99]] which did not have a winter break, meaning teams had to play throughout January. The break was abolished to avoid fixture congestion caused by more Scottish clubs participating in [[UEFA]] competitions and the [[2002 FIFA World Cup|upcoming FIFA World Cup]].<ref name="Winter break">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/1097393.stm|title=SPL may scrap 2002 winter break|work=[[BBC Sport]]|date=2 January 2001|access-date=6 February 2018}}</ref> This change was criticised by many SPL managers, including [[Martin O'Neill]]<ref name="McLeish winter break">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/r/rangers/2884453.stm|title=McLeish berates SPL|work=[[BBC Sport]]|date=25 March 2003|access-date=6 February 2018}}</ref> and [[Alex McLeish]].<ref name="McLeish winter break"/>

===European berths===
Results in European competition over the previous five years saw the league move down from 15th to 16th in the [[UEFA coefficient#Men's Association coefficient|UEFA country coefficient]] ranking. This meant that the league lost one of its berths in the [[UEFA Champions League]] qualifying rounds for the following season, and received an additional berth in the [[2002–03 UEFA Cup]] qualifying round.<ref name="UEFA country ranking">{{cite news|url=https://kassiesa.home.xs4all.nl/bert/uefa/history/qual2002.html|publisher=Bert Kassies|title=Qualification for European club football 2002/03|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=16 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180816120632/http://kassiesa.home.xs4all.nl/bert/uefa/history/qual2002.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Teams==
Twelve clubs participated in the league in the 2001–02 season – the top eleven clubs in the [[2000–01 Scottish Premier League]] and the champions of the [[2000–01 Scottish First Division]].

[[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] were relegated from the top flight after only one season of participation. They were replaced by [[Livingston F.C.|Livingston]], who secured the First Division title and promotion to the SPL with a 3–2 victory away to [[Inverness Caledonian Thistle F.C.|Inverness Caledonian Thistle]] on 28 April 2001.<ref name="Livi promoted">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_div_1/1301999.stm|title=Livvy wrap up the title|work=[[BBC Sport]]|date=28 April 2001|access-date=6 February 2018}}</ref> This would be Livingston's first season at the top level of [[Football in Scotland|Scottish football]] in their 58-year history.

==Overview==
The 2001–02 season would be a record-breaking season for [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]], who won consecutive titles for the first time since they won the title in both [[1980–81 Scottish Premier Division|1981]] and [[1981–82 Scottish Premier Division|1982]]. Celtic accrued the most points in a season of any team in the SPL era (103), achieved the most wins in a season (33), conceded the fewest goals (18) and lost the fewest games (their sole defeat at [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]] in December <ref name="Celtic defeat">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/1721802.stm|title=Dons sink champions|date=22 December 2001|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref>). They also went unbeaten at home for the entire league season – a run that would extend through the entirety of the [[2002–03 Scottish Premier League|following season]], for 77 matches, until a defeat to Aberdeen on 21 April 2004.<ref name="Aberdeen beat Celtic">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/3643021.stm|title=Celtic 1-2 Aberdeen|date=21 April 2004|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref> The only points Celtic dropped at home was in their final home game, an [[Old Firm]] derby against [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] which was drawn 1–1.<ref name="Celtic 1–1 Rangers">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/1939522.stm|title=Old Firm end all square|date=21 April 2002|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref> Celtic clinched the title at [[Celtic Park]] on 6 April 2002, with a 5–1 win against [[Livingston F.C.|Livingston]].<ref name="Celtic win title"/> [[Henrik Larsson]] again finished as the league's top scorer, with 29 goals.

[[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] started the season poorly and were 11 points behind Celtic when manager [[Dick Advocaat]] stepped aside and [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]] manager [[Alex McLeish]] was appointed to replace him.<ref name="McLeish Rangers manager"/> However, Rangers still finished a distant 2nd, 18 points adrift of Celtic. They did, however, win the [[2001–02 Scottish Cup|Scottish Cup]] and the [[2001–02 Scottish League Cup|League Cup]], beating Celtic<ref name="Scottish Cup final">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scottish_cup/1966673.stm|title=Rangers win Old Firm final|date=4 May 2002|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref> and [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]]<ref name="League Cup final">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/cis_ins_cup/1875551.stm|title=Rangers lift CIS Cup|date=17 March 2002|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref> in the finals, respectively. They also reached the last 16 of the [[2001–02 UEFA Cup|UEFA Cup]], losing narrowly to eventual winners [[Feyenoord]].<ref name="Feyenoord">{{cite news|url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/match/68829--feyenoord-vs-rangers/|title=UEFA Europa League Archive|access-date=7 February 2018|publisher=[[UEFA]]}}</ref>

Alex McLeish's replacement at Hibernian was fan-favourite<ref name="Sauzee poll">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/football_focus/4416093.stm|title=Hibernian's cult heroes|date=8 April 2005|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref> [[Franck Sauzée]],<ref name="Sauzee appointment"/> who retired from playing to take the management role. However, he was sacked after only two months and 15 matches,<ref name="Sauzee sacked"/> having been eliminated from the [[2001–02 Scottish League Cup|League Cup]] in a shock loss to Ayr United, and the team second from bottom in the table. Hibernian did not win a league match with Sauzée in charge. Sauzée served as manager for the shortest time of [[List of Hibernian F.C. managers|any manager in Hibernian's history]] (69 days). Sauzée was replaced by [[Bobby Williamson]], who led the team to safety in 10th place.

Newly promoted [[Livingston F.C.|Livingston]], under [[Jim Leishman]], confounded pundits by finishing their first ever season in the top league in third-place, earning a spot in the [[2002–03 UEFA Cup]].

The 2001–02 season was the first in which the financial situation of SPL clubs was questioned.<ref name="Scotsman report">{{cite news|url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/competitions/premiership/game-on-the-brink-of-bankruptcy-1-620983|newspaper=[[The Scotsman]]|title=Game on the brink of bankruptcy|date=12 September 2002|access-date=7 February 2018}}</ref> Total debt among all twelve SPL clubs was estimated during 2001&ndash;02 to be around £132m, having been barely into double figures two years previously.<ref name="Scotsman report"/> The end of television coverage from [[Sky Sports]] caused multiple clubs in the league to suffer severe financial difficulties.<ref name="Motherwell crisis"/>
In pre-season, [[Motherwell F.C.|Motherwell]] lost a number of players, including [[Andy Goram]] and [[Lee McCulloch]], in an attempt to reduce the clubs wage bill.<ref name="Davies leaves Motherwell"/> Manager [[Billy Davies]] also resigned early on in the season.<ref name="Davies leaves Motherwell"/> Motherwell became the first SPL club to enter administration in April 2002, with debts of £11 million and a wage bill totalling 97% of the club's annual turnover.<ref name="Motherwell crisis"/> Davies' replacement, [[Eric Black]], and chief executive [[Pat Nevin]] both left their roles with only two matches to go of the season once administration hit,<ref name="Motherwell crisis"/> and 19 of the club's players were made redundant at the end of the season.<ref name="Motherwell axe 19 players">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/m/motherwell/1958230.stm|title=Motherwell axe 19 players|work=[[BBC Sport]]|date=29 April 2002|access-date=7 February 2002}}</ref>

Despite Motherwell's financial difficulties, it was [[St Johnstone F.C.|St Johnstone]] who finished the season as the bottom team in the league, with only 21 points, 19 points behind 11th place. Their relegation to the [[2002–03 Scottish First Division|First Division]] was confirmed on 6 April 2002, after a 1–1 draw against Motherwell left them 14 points adrift with 4 matches to play.<ref name="Saints relegated">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_prem/1913011.stm|title=Well condemn sad Saints|date=5 April 2002|access-date=7 February 2018|work=[[BBC Sport]]}}</ref>

==Format==
In the initial phase of the season, each of the twelve teams play the other eleven teams three times. After 33 rounds, the league splits into two sections, a top six and a bottom six, with each team playing all the other teams in their section once. The league attempts to balance the fixture list so that teams in the same section have played each other twice at home and twice away, but sometimes this is impossible. A total of 228 matches will be played, with 38 matches played by each team.
